title: India Has Rejected Washington's 'Forced Labour' and 'Surplus Capacity' Charges. The 12.5 Per Cent Tariff Threat Is Now Part of the Deal.
excerpt: As USTR Jamieson Greer prepares to fly to India the week after the G7, New Delhi is pushing for an assurance that no new tariffs will follow the bilateral trade agreement. Both sides say mid-July is possible.
body:
The United States has proposed a 12.5 per cent tariff surcharge on Indian goods, citing what it calls the use of forced labour. It has separately floated additional duties on Indian textiles and steel, alleging surplus production capacity that is harming American industry. India has rejected both charges.

What makes this confrontation significant is not the accusations themselves — they are well-worn instruments of American trade policy — but the fact that both sides now acknowledge they are being folded into the broader bilateral trade agreement that could be concluded as early as mid-July.

"Certainly an element of the negotiation," is how Atul Keshap, president of the US-India Business Council and a former diplomat with 30 years in government, described the forced-labour tariff proposal in a recent interview. He argued that in bilateral talks, "all of these various elements are part of the main negotiation."

The Charges

The forced-labour tariff, proposed this month under a Section 301 investigation, would apply an additional 12.5 per cent on imports from India and several other countries. India's Commerce Ministry has pushed back firmly, noting that the charges have not been finalised and that New Delhi is engaging with Washington through the formal investigation process.

The surplus-capacity allegation targets textiles and steel — sectors where India is a major global exporter. Piyush Goyal's Commerce Ministry has called the characterisation misleading, with a senior trade official telling Reuters that the move appeared aimed at "a particular country while also serving other trade-related aims."

"India's Trade Minister Piyush Goyal said both sides were "moving swiftly" toward finalising the first tranche of a bilateral trade agreement, possibly by mid-July."

India's position is that its textile exports are driven by competitive advantage, not state-subsidised overproduction, and that its steel output serves domestic infrastructure demand first.

The Deal Takes Shape

Despite the friction, both governments are signalling urgency. USTR Jamieson Greer will travel to India the week after the G7 summit in Evian, a senior US administration official confirmed on Saturday. Trade will be discussed when President Trump meets Prime Minister Modi on the summit sidelines, but no agreement is expected there.

The real action will happen in New Delhi. A US delegation led by Assistant USTR Brendan Lynch held three days of talks with Indian officials last week. India's Trade Minister Piyush Goyal said both sides were "moving swiftly" toward finalising the first tranche of a bilateral trade agreement, possibly by mid-July.

The deal, as currently structured, would reduce US tariffs on most Indian goods to 18 per cent from the current 50 per cent. India would slash tariffs on American industrial goods to zero from 13.5 per cent and eliminate duties on a range of agricultural products — tree nuts, wine, spirits, fruits, and vegetables — though protections on sensitive commodities like rice, dairy, and sugar would remain.

India is also seeking an assurance that the deal would shield it from future tariff actions — a request that reflects deep frustration in New Delhi over the unpredictability of American trade policy under Trump.

What's at Stake for the Diaspora

For the roughly 4.4 million Indian Americans and the tens of thousands of Indian businesses that operate across the US-India trade corridor, the outcome matters directly. A successful deal would bring the first formal trade agreement between the two countries in 75 years — something Keshap called "woefully overdue."

The current bilateral trade relationship, at roughly $200 billion annually, is "woefully underpowered," Keshap said, arguing that a deal could push it toward the $500 billion mark. Without one, he warned, the relationship is on a "more rocky path."

The forced-labour and surplus-capacity allegations, if left unresolved, could trigger the additional tariffs regardless of any broader deal. India is betting that by wrapping them into the negotiation, it can neutralise both threats at once. Washington appears willing to play along — for now.

The Timeline

Modi and Trump meet at the G7 in Evian on Wednesday. Greer arrives in New Delhi the following week. Indian officials have told Reuters that a deal can be finalised after the Section 301 investigation concludes — but only if the resulting tariff rate is "competitive with direct competitors."

The next six weeks will determine whether the world's largest democracy and the world's largest economy can finally formalise a trade relationship that both sides acknowledge has been running on goodwill and improvisation for decades.
